The Kings of the Romans.
Now Maximian, although unwillingly, stopped the persecution;
and after a little while he invented [a pretext],
saying that the gods had revealed to him that it was right that the Christians should be driven out from the cities and the country-places {OCR?}.
And when the persecution was again stirred up,
God chastised the earth with famine and pestilence,
so that a modius of wheat was sold for two hundred and fifty obols (minas?),
and ten corpses were cast into one grave.
And this Maximian, while {OCR?} he was occupied {OCR?} in the war with the Armenians,
the rod of justice overtook him,
and he was smitten with a grievous disease,
and he also died along with Diocletian.
[Constantine the Great (Constantius?)] who in the days of Diocletian was king in Gaul,
and he is the father of Constantine the Victorious.
And when he reigned,
he had two wives:
one, Helena, the mother of Constantine the Victorious,
and the other, Theodora, the daughter of Maximian the tyrant.
And this Constantine the Great (Constantius?), Sylvester, bishop of Rome, made him a disciple,
because he was a leper;
and he believed and was baptized and was healed.
Now he reigned twelve years;
and when in the eighth year of his reign, he set up for himself {OCR?} as partner in his kingdom his own son Constantine the Victorious {OCR?}.
[Constantine the Victorious reigned] thirty-two years,
apart from the three years that he reigned with his father.
